passage: Zeenat lost the district badminton final in straight sets, in front of the whole school contingent. Then the rain came down so hard the buses couldn't leave, and she was stuck in the sports complex for two hours with everyone who had watched. She sat on the steps by the vending machine, towel over her head, wishing she could vanish. Someone sat down beside her. Devika. She didn't say 'it's okay' or 'you'll win next time'. She said, 'I still think you're the best player in our school. One match doesn't change that.' Then she opened a packet of chips and held it out. Zeenat laughed shakily and took one. Her shoulders came down from her ears. They watched the rain together until the buses came. A month later Devika forgot her lines in the inter-house drama. Zeenat was the first one backstage, sitting beside her with chips.

qa.q: How long was Zeenat stuck in the sports complex?
qa.a: Two hours, because the rain was so heavy the buses couldn't leave.

qa.q: What does Zeenat's shoulders coming down suggest?
qa.a: It suggests relief, as Devika's words eased her shame after the loss 😊

qa.q: How did Zeenat return the kindness?
qa.a: When Devika forgot her lines, Zeenat was first backstage, sitting beside her with chips.

qa.q: How does Devika see Zeenat after the loss?
qa.a: She still sees her as the best player in school; one match doesn't change her respect.

grounding: Shows a teen who loses publicly and feels relief when a friend sits by her with respect, later doing the same for that friend.

passage: The school quiz final in the Pune auditorium came down to the last question, and Siddharth buzzed too early. Wrong answer. The other team won by five points, and his own team walked off without looking at him. He sat alone in the last row of the empty auditorium, jaw clenched, replaying the buzz. Nirmala found him there. She slid into the seat next to him. 'You carried us to the final, Sid. I still respect you. Okay, that sounded like a speech. But it's true.' He laughed despite himself, and felt his throat loosen. He didn't argue with her. He just said, 'Thanks. I needed that.' They stayed until the watchman rattled his keys. Two weeks later, Nirmala's science model collapsed in front of the judges. Siddharth was there with a roll of tape and the same words.

qa.q: Where did Nirmala find Siddharth after the final?
qa.a: In the last row of the empty auditorium.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when Nirmala sat beside him?
qa.a: His throat loosened with relief after the shame of the early buzz.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do right when Nirmala comforted him?
qa.a: He accepted the comfort instead of arguing, simply saying thanks and that he needed it 🙂

qa.q: How does Nirmala see Siddharth's early buzz?
qa.a: She sees one mistake from the person who carried the team to the final.

grounding: Shows a teen who loses a quiz final, accepts a friend's respect and comfort with relief, and later does the same for her.

passage: Xin touched the wall and looked up at the board: two seconds slower than her personal best. Worse, Coach Tariq was standing at the end of the lane with his arms crossed and a frown she couldn't read. She climbed out, cheeks burning, sure he'd given up on her. In the changing room she almost left without speaking to him. Then she thought: if I don't ask, I'll just make up the worst answer. She found him by the stands of the Richmond pool, still frowning at his clipboard. 'Coach, what should I work on?' He looked up, surprised, and the frown eased. 'Your turns, Xin. You lost a second on each. Your stroke was strong.' He sketched the turn on the clipboard. 'And I wasn't frowning at you. I was frowning at myself. I should have caught this in training.' Xin laughed, half relieved. 'Tuesday, then? Turns?' 'Tuesday.'

qa.q: Where did Xin lose time, according to Coach Tariq?
qa.a: On her turns; she lost a second on each.

qa.q: What was Xin feeling when she saw the coach frowning?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and afraid, sure he had given up on her.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Xin, and why?
qa.a: Asking the coach what to work on, because it turned a scary frown into a clear fix 👍

qa.q: What was Coach Tariq actually frowning about?
qa.a: Himself, for not catching the turns problem in training.

grounding: Shows a teen facing a coach's frown after a poor result who asks what to learn and finds it wasn't a total rejection.

passage: When Pallavi Ma'am handed back the maths test, she didn't smile at Jasleen the way she usually did. She just put the paper down, 11 out of 40, and moved on. Jasleen stared at the red marks. Ma'am's face said it all, she thought. She thinks I'm useless now. All through the next period Jasleen's stomach churned, and she wondered about switching to the other section. At the bell she forced herself to the staffroom door instead. 'Ma'am, can I ask what I should do differently?' Pallavi Ma'am took off her glasses. 'I was disappointed, Jasleen, I won't lie. Not in you. In the result, because I know what you can do. You rushed the word problems. Look.' She circled three questions where Jasleen had skipped a step. 'Come to the Thursday clinic. Bring these.' Jasleen walked out lighter. A frown about one test wasn't a verdict on her.

qa.q: What score did Jasleen get on the maths test?
qa.a: 11 out of 40.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling through the next period?
qa.a: She felt anxious and rejected, her stomach churning, sure Ma'am thought she was useless.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do instead of switching sections?
qa.a: She went to the staffroom and asked what to do differently, and got specific help.

qa.q: How does Pallavi Ma'am see the test result?
qa.a: She is disappointed in the result, not in Jasleen, because she knows what Jasleen can do.

grounding: Shows a teen who reads a teacher's disappointment as rejection, then asks what to learn and finds the frown was about the result.

passage:
Hi Zubin,
You asked how I'm doing after the Olympiad. Honestly? Crushed for a week. I'd studied every night for three months and didn't even make the second round.
Then Papa told me something. One of the scientists whose photo is up in our physics lab failed her entrance exam twice before she got in. Nobody puts that on the poster.
So I've made a smaller plan. Not 'do everything'. Just twenty problems a week, and on Sundays I redo the ones I got wrong and write down why. Last Sunday I found I keep making the same mistake with units. The same one! Fixing that alone got me five more marks on the class test.
It's slower. It's boring. It's working.
Next year's Olympiad is in eleven months. I'm not promising I'll win. I'm promising I'll beat this year's me.
How's your music exam prep going? Send me your plan and I'll send you mine.
Sonali

qa.q: What mistake did Sonali keep making?
qa.a: The same mistake with units.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel in the week after the Olympiad?
qa.a: Sonali felt crushed and disappointed after months of nightly study.

qa.q: Why is Sonali's smaller plan a good one?
qa.a: Twenty problems a week plus Sunday corrections turns failure into steady practice and fixing mistakes, and it's already working 👍

qa.q: How might Zubin feel reading the email?
qa.a: Zubin may feel encouraged to make a small plan too, since Sonali offers to swap plans.

grounding: An email from a teen who failed an Olympiad and restarts with a smaller plan of practice and correction, remembering that known achievers fail quietly too.

passage: Trisha, you keep asking why I'm up at six with the harmonium. Fine. I'm Vandana, and I bombed the music scholarship audition in April. Voice cracked on the high note, in front of three judges. I came home and said I'm never singing again. That lasted two weeks. Then my guruji told me something: every singer she admires has a list of auditions they failed; they just don't post it. So I made a small plan. Not three hours a day like before, when I'd get tired and quit. Twenty minutes every morning. Five on scales, fifteen on that one high note. I record it and listen back in the evening, and write down one thing to fix. Just one. Some mornings it's still awful. But last week I hit it clean, twice. The next audition's in December. I don't know if I'll get it. I do know I'll be better than April.

qa.q: How long does Vandana practise every morning now?
qa.a: Twenty minutes: five on scales and fifteen on the high note.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling after the audition in April?
qa.a: Vandana felt humiliated and defeated, enough to swear off singing for two weeks.

qa.q: What makes the new plan better than the old one?
qa.a: It is small enough to keep up and includes recording and fixing one thing, so practice leads to correction.

qa.q: How does guruji see failed auditions?
qa.a: As something every admired singer has, just not something they post.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen who failed an audition and restarts with a small daily plan of practice and correction.

passage: Tanvir, you're sulking because Rehaan posted your match score with a laughing face. Let me tell you your Mohit Chacha's own story. At sixteen I lost the state chess semi-final in eleven moves. Eleven. My rival Dinesh, whom I'd beaten twice, went round the hall telling everyone, and later wrote on the notice board, 'Mohit, try ludo.' I wanted to write something worse under it. I even had the chalk in my hand. Then my coach, old Mr Pinto, took the chalk away. He said, 'A boy who has to shout his win is not sure of it. Your opponent is on the chessboard, not on this board.' So I went home and replayed those eleven moves forty times till I saw my mistake. The next year I didn't beat Dinesh. I beat my own rating by two hundred points. That felt better, Tanvir. You'll see.

qa.q: What did Dinesh write on the notice board?
qa.a: 'Mohit, try ludo.'

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling with the chalk in his hand?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and angry, tempted to write something even worse in revenge.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mohit's story?
qa.a: Mr Pinto taking the chalk away, and Mohit then studying the eleven moves to beat his own rating.

qa.q: How did Mr Pinto see Dinesh's gloating?
qa.a: As a sign Dinesh wasn't sure of his win, since he needed to shout about it.

grounding: An elder's story of a rival gloating over a loss, choosing not to stoop, and working to beat his own past score.

passage: The robot stalled halfway across the arena floor, and the timer ran out with Zubin's team in last place. Worse, the next round started in forty minutes, and there was only one charging point, which Uday's team was hogging. 'Maybe build a toy car next time,' Uday said, loud enough for the queue, and his teammates snorted. Zubin felt his face go hot. A comeback about Uday's wobbly arm design was right there on his tongue. He swallowed it. Anyone who needs to crow that loudly, he thought, must be pretty nervous himself. Instead he knelt by the robot with his teammate Asha, found the loose wire in the left motor, and taped it with their last strip. There was no time to charge fully. In the second round the robot crossed the line, slower than Uday's, but twelve seconds faster than their own morning run. Asha high-fived him. That was the number that mattered.

qa.q: What problem did Zubin find in the robot?
qa.a: A loose wire in the left motor.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when Uday made the toy car comment?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and angry, his face hot, with a comeback ready on his tongue.

qa.q: What did Zubin choose instead of hitting back?
qa.a: He swallowed the comeback and fixed the robot, focusing on beating his own morning time.

qa.q: What might Uday's loud gloating say about him?
qa.a: That he might be nervous himself, needing to crow to feel secure.

grounding: Shows a teen whose rival gloats after a failure, choosing not to stoop and focusing on beating his own earlier score.

passage: Hansa never raised her hand in class unless she was completely sure. At the new pottery club in the Bandra community hall, she watched Rehana's lopsided bowl collapse on the wheel, heard her laugh, and kept her own hands firmly in her lap. 'Your turn,' Rehana said. 'I'll just watch this week.' Hansa had said that for three weeks. Walking home along the sea wall, she did the maths. Three weeks of watching. Zero bowls. Rehana had five ugly ones and one that almost held water. Hansa realised that being scared of a bad bowl had cost her more than any bad bowl could. The next Saturday she asked the teacher for a lump of clay 'just to squish, not to keep'. Her first bowl slumped sideways like a tired dog. Rehana laughed, and so did Hansa, surprising herself. The second one stood up.

qa.q: How many bowls had Rehana made by the time Hansa counted?
qa.a: Five ugly ones and one that almost held water.

qa.q: Why did Hansa keep her hands in her lap?
qa.a: She felt afraid of making a bad bowl and being seen to fail.

qa.q: What low-stakes step helped Hansa start?
qa.a: Asking for clay 'just to squish, not to keep', so the first try didn't have to be good.

qa.q: How does Rehana see her own collapsing bowls?
qa.a: She laughs at them, treating failure as part of learning rather than something to fear 🙂

grounding: Shows a teen who avoids trying for fear of failing, realising the fear costs more, and starting with a low-stakes attempt.

passage:
'Just submit one drawing,' Vaibhav said, tapping the magazine notice. 'Deadline's Friday.'
'No. They're not good enough.'
'You've filled four sketchbooks, Trisha.'
'Exactly. Four sketchbooks nobody's seen. If nobody sees them, nobody can say they're bad.'
'And nobody can say they're good either.'
Trisha frowned. 'That's annoyingly true.'
'What's the worst that happens?'
'They reject it. Everyone knows. I die.'
'Nobody reads a rejection list. There isn't one.'
She laughed despite herself. 'Fine. What's the smallest version of this?'
'Pin one sketch on the art club board. No name, if you want. See what happens.'
'No name.' She flipped through the book and tore out the crow on the electric wire. 'This one. It's not perfect.'
'Nothing on that board is perfect. That's why it's there.'
By Friday, three people had written 'who drew the crow?' on sticky notes beside it.

qa.q: Which sketch did Trisha pick for the art club board?
qa.a: The crow on the electric wire.

qa.q: What was Trisha afraid of about submitting a drawing?
qa.a: She feared rejection so much that keeping the sketchbooks hidden felt safer than risking being called bad.

qa.q: Why was the anonymous board a good first step?
qa.a: It was low-stakes, so Trisha could test sharing without her name or a rejection on the line.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see the four hidden sketchbooks?
qa.a: As wasted chances, since nobody can call them good if nobody sees them.

grounding: Shows a teen who won't share her art for fear of failing, and starts with a low-stakes anonymous post.

passage: I still remember walking home with my Class 9 result folded small in my pocket, as if making it tiny would make the maths mark smaller too. I'm Sumit, and I had failed maths after telling Papa for weeks that it was 'going fine'. At home my little sister Mehak was doing her homework, and Papa looked up from his newspaper. I put the paper on the table and waited for the shouting. It didn't come. He read it, folded it and said, 'Come, sit. You must have been carrying this alone for a while.' I cried then, properly. He let me. When I could talk, I told him the truth: I'd been lost since the algebra chapter and too embarrassed to say. He didn't lecture. He asked what would help. We made a plan together: extra help on Saturdays, and every Friday I'd tell him how the week went, good or bad. I passed the retest. Mostly I remember feeling safe.

qa.q: What did Papa say after reading the result?
qa.a: 'Come, sit. You must have been carrying this alone for a while.'

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling while waiting for Papa's reaction?
qa.a: Sumit felt scared and ashamed, expecting shouting after weeks of saying it was 'going fine'.

qa.q: What did Sumit and Papa plan together?
qa.a: Extra help on Saturdays, and a Friday check-in about how the week went, good or bad.

qa.q: How does Papa see Sumit's failed maths paper?
qa.a: As a heavy secret his child carried alone, calling for comfort and a plan rather than a scolding.

grounding: A first-person memory of a parent comforting instead of scolding after a failed exam, leading to honest sharing and a shared plan.

passage: Coach's note, Sunday, under-16 cup semi-final. Farhan scored an own goal in the 80th minute and we went out 1-0. He walked off with his shirt pulled over his face while Tejas and the others stood around, not knowing what to do. I saw his mother come down from the stands and braced myself; some parents get upset. Instead she sat next to him on the bench, put an arm round him and said something quietly. After a minute his shoulders stopped shaking. Later he came to me and told me honestly what had happened: he'd lost the ball in the sun and panicked. His mother stood with him while he explained and asked what he could work on. We agreed on extra drills on calling for the ball, on Wednesdays, and she offered to drive him. I've made a note to check in with him at Tuesday training.

qa.q: Why did the team go out of the cup?
qa.a: Farhan scored an own goal in the 80th minute and they lost 1-0.

qa.q: What does Farhan hiding under his shirt suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt ashamed and devastated after the own goal.

qa.q: What next step did Farhan, his mother and the coach agree on?
qa.a: Extra drills on calling for the ball on Wednesdays, with his mother driving him.

qa.q: What might have changed if Farhan's mother had scolded him?
qa.a: He might have hidden what happened instead of explaining honestly and planning the next step.

grounding: A coach's note showing a teen comforted by his mother after a public failure, then sharing honestly and planning the next step together.

passage: Every day at the government school in Rampur, Vikas watched his best friend Naveen take the tiffin of a small Class 6 boy, Gopal, and eat the parathas behind the water tank. Gopal had started crying on the way to school. Vikas felt sick about it, but Naveen was the one who'd stood up for him back in Class 5. Telling felt like betrayal. On Monday, walking home past the sugarcane fields, Vikas said, 'Leave Gopal alone, yaar. He's tiny. It's not funny.' Naveen shrugged. 'Just parathas.' On Wednesday it happened again, and this time Gopal had a scraped knee from being pushed. Vikas went to Master ji after the prayer bell and told him everything. Master ji thanked him, sat with Gopal that same morning, and called Naveen's father to school after lunch. Naveen didn't talk to Vikas for a week. Then, at the handpump, he muttered, 'You were right.'

qa.q: Where did Naveen eat Gopal's parathas?
qa.a: Behind the water tank.

qa.q: Why did Vikas feel torn about reporting Naveen?
qa.a: He felt sick about the bullying, but guilty at the idea of betraying the friend who once stood up for him.

qa.q: Which steps did Vikas take, and why was that order wise?
qa.a: He talked to Naveen first, and when Gopal got hurt he told Master ji, because the harm kept going.

qa.q: How might Gopal have felt before Vikas spoke up?
qa.a: Scared and helpless, crying on the way to school and then hurt as well.

grounding: Shows a teen torn between loyalty and right who talks to a bullying friend first, then tells a teacher when the harm continues.

passage: In the library at their school in Malmö, Ulla saw it on Siddiq's screen before he could close the tab: photos of next week's chemistry exam, posted in a paid group. 'Where did you get that?' she whispered. He grinned nervously. 'Someone's cousin. Everyone's buying it. Want me to send it?' Ulla's stomach dropped. Siddiq had helped her through every lab this year; she didn't want to be the one who got him in trouble. 'Please don't use it,' she said. 'If you get caught, you're finished. And it's not fair on everyone else.' He said he'd think about it. The next day she saw him forwarding the photos to three more people. That evening Ulla emailed her form tutor, Ms Berg, with what she had seen. Ms Berg replied within the hour, thanked her, and said the exam would be replaced and the group reported, without naming Ulla. Siddiq was angry for a while. Ulla still thought she'd done right.

qa.q: What did Ulla see on Siddiq's screen?
qa.a: Photos of next week's chemistry exam, posted in a paid group.

qa.q: What was Ulla feeling when Siddiq offered to send the photos?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped; she felt torn between loyalty to Siddiq and knowing it was wrong.

qa.q: Why did Ulla email Ms Berg the next day?
qa.a: Talking to Siddiq hadn't worked and he was spreading the photos, so the unfairness was growing and an adult needed to act.

qa.q: How might other students see the replaced exam?
qa.a: They would likely find it fairer, even if they never knew why it changed.

grounding: Shows a teen who talks to a cheating friend first and, when he keeps spreading the leaked exam, tells a teacher.

passage: Since Mridul told the hostel warden about the seniors making juniors do push-ups at midnight, the second-floor corridor had gone silent around him. His roommates dragged their mattresses to the next room. Someone had written SNITCH on his locker in marker. At dinner in the mess he sat alone with his dal, his throat so tight he couldn't swallow. Maybe they were right. Maybe he'd ruined everything. On Saturday the house mistress, Mrs Vasudha Iyer, stopped him outside the mess. 'I heard about the locker. I've had it cleaned, and I've spoken to your floor. How are you, really?' 'I just wanted them to stop hurting the little ones,' he said. 'Not to get anyone punished.' 'That's the difference,' she said. 'You spoke up to protect, not to hurt.' She introduced him to two juniors from the debate club who had been made to do the push-ups. They saved him a seat every night after that.

qa.q: What was written on Mridul's locker?
qa.a: SNITCH, in marker.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling at dinner in the mess?
qa.a: He felt hurt and lonely, his throat too tight to swallow, wondering if he had ruined everything.

qa.q: What helped Mridul most after being frozen out?
qa.a: The house mistress checking on him, naming the difference between protecting and punishing, and connecting him with allies.

qa.q: How might the juniors see Mridul's report?
qa.a: As protection from midnight punishment, which is why they saved him a seat every night.

grounding: Shows a teen frozen out as a snitch after reporting ragging, recognising he spoke up to protect, and finding allies.

passage:
Dear Naveen Bhaiya,
You told me to write when things got bad, so here it is.
Two weeks ago I told our class teacher that Sanya's photo, the one she sent only to one friend, was being passed around the class group. I didn't name anyone to get them punished. I just wanted it deleted before it went further.
Since then my group won't sit with me. They call me 'teacher's spy' in the corridor. They left me out of a birthday plan on purpose, and I found out from a story. I cry in the bathroom at break. It really hurts.
But yesterday Sanya found me by the library and said thank you. She said the photo was gone because of me. And Ma'am has checked on me twice.
I keep telling myself: I spoke up to protect Sanya, not to hurt anyone. That's different from snitching. Some days I believe it.
Can you call on Sunday? I need someone on my side.
Mahima

qa.q: What does the group call Mahima in the corridor?
qa.a: 'Teacher's spy'.

qa.q: How has being frozen out made Mahima feel?
qa.a: Mahima feels deeply hurt and lonely, crying in the bathroom at break.

qa.q: What helps Mahima hold on to the choice to report?
qa.a: Remembering it was to protect Sanya, not punish anyone, plus Sanya's thanks and reaching out to Naveen Bhaiya.

qa.q: How does Sanya see what Mahima did?
qa.a: She is grateful, since the photo was deleted because Mahima spoke up.

grounding: A letter from a teen frozen out after reporting a shared private photo, holding on to the protective reason for telling and finding allies.

passage: Last term I found out that Lavanya, who sits behind me, was being followed from the bus stop by two older boys who kept filming her and making comments. She'd started taking a longer route home. My first thought was to get my cousins and 'sort them out'. Looking back, I'm glad I didn't. At the end of that same day I went to Mr Fernandes, the class teacher everyone trusts. I'd written down the facts: which bus stop, what time, what the boys looked like, what Lavanya had told our friends. I asked him not to say it came from me, and he promised. He called Lavanya in gently that afternoon with the counsellor and phoned her parents before evening. The school also informed the police beat officer near the stop. A week later I asked him if it was being handled. It was. The boys stopped coming. I'm Manoj, and I learned that telling the right person does more than any fight.

qa.q: What details did Manoj write down before going to Mr Fernandes?
qa.a: Which bus stop, what time, what the boys looked like, and what Lavanya had told friends.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling on first hearing about the boys?
qa.a: Manoj felt angry and protective, wanting to get cousins to 'sort them out' before choosing a safer path.

qa.q: What did Manoj do that made the report effective?
qa.a: Gave clear facts, asked for confidentiality, reported the same day, and followed up a week later.

qa.q: How might Lavanya have felt once the school stepped in?
qa.a: Likely relieved and safer, able to stop taking the long route home.

grounding: A first-person account of reporting a classmate's harassment to a trusted teacher with facts and a confidentiality request, then following up.

passage: Class teacher's note, 9 November. At the end of lunch Shalini waited until the room was empty and asked if she could tell me something 'without anyone knowing it came from me'. She had screenshots on her phone: for two weeks a group of boys from 10B had been posting comments about Sarika's body in their chat and leaving notes in her bag. Shalini had already listed the dates. She said she'd thought about confronting them herself and decided it would only make things worse for Sarika. I thanked her, agreed to keep her name out of it, and forwarded the screenshots to our safeguarding lead, Mrs Pinto, within the hour. Mrs Pinto met Sarika with the counsellor that afternoon and called both families by evening; the boys were spoken to the next morning. On Friday Shalini asked me whether it had been handled. I told her yes, and that her careful report had made it possible.

qa.q: What had Shalini already listed before reporting?
qa.a: The dates of the comments and notes.

qa.q: Why did Shalini ask to stay anonymous?
qa.a: She felt worried about backlash and wanted to protect herself and Sarika while still getting help.

qa.q: Why was Shalini's choice not to confront the boys wise?
qa.a: Confronting them herself could have made things worse for Sarika; a trusted adult could act safely.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt when the counsellor met her?
qa.a: Probably relieved and less alone, knowing adults were acting on the harassment.

grounding: A teacher's note on a teen reporting a classmate's harassment with facts and a confidentiality request, then following up.

passage: Tuition centre note, Parveen Khan, Tuesday. Manoj (Class 10) came in today pale and silent. After class he told me that two weeks ago he reported to his class teacher that older boys were taking money from juniors in the washroom. Instead of acting, the teacher told those boys who had complained. Since then they've shoved him in the corridor and written his name on the washroom wall. He said, 'I did the right thing and the school made it worse.' He feels betrayed, and he's frightened. I told him he was right to report and none of this is his fault. With his permission we wrote down dates, names and what happened, and I phoned his mother, who came to the centre. Tonight we emailed the principal directly and copied the school management. I gave him the child helpline number. His mother will walk him to school tomorrow. I'll check in with him on Thursday.

qa.q: What was written on the washroom wall?
qa.a: Manoj's name.

qa.q: How does Manoj feel about the school's response?
qa.a: He feels betrayed and frightened, since reporting made things worse.

qa.q: What steps did Parveen Khan and Manoj's mother take?
qa.a: They documented dates and names, emailed the principal and management that night, gave the helpline number, and arranged for him to be walked to school.

qa.q: How might the juniors see the school's failure to act?
qa.a: They may feel even less safe, learning that reporting might not protect them.

grounding: A tuition teacher's note on a teen who feels betrayed after a school exposed his report, helping him document, escalate and stay safe.

passage:
Friday. I'm so angry I can't sleep. Two weeks ago I told Mr Gupta that Ramesh and his friends keep threatening me at the cycle stand, saying they'll 'fix' me after school. He said, 'Boys will be boys, ignore them.' Today they pushed my cycle into the drain and said next time it'll be me. So the school basically did nothing. I trusted them and they let me down. Tonight I finally told Amma and Appa everything. I thought Appa would shout at me for not telling earlier, but he just said, 'You tried the right way. Now we try the next way.' We wrote down every date and what was said, and I found the photo of my bent cycle. Appa emailed the principal tonight and wrote that if nothing happens by Monday, he'll go to the school board. Amma saved the child helpline number in my phone. Appa will drop me to school until this is sorted. I feel a bit safer.
- Jeevan

qa.q: What did Mr Gupta say when Jeevan reported the threats?
qa.a: 'Boys will be boys, ignore them.'

qa.q: What is Jeevan feeling after the school ignored the report?
qa.a: Jeevan feels angry and let down, too upset to sleep after trusting the school.

qa.q: What did Jeevan and the parents do next?
qa.a: They documented dates and the bent cycle photo, emailed the principal with a plan to go to the board, saved the helpline number, and arranged drop-offs.

qa.q: How does Appa see Jeevan's first report to Mr Gupta?
qa.a: As the right way to try first, not a mistake; now it's time for the next step.

grounding: A diary of a teen whose report of threats was ignored, feeling betrayed, then documenting and escalating with parents while staying safe.
